newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Doubts raised over N.Korea nuclear power ability.
newsitem.headline: Doubts raised over N.Korea nuclear power ability.

text.p: Plans to build two nuclear power stations in North Korea raised serious doubts about the ability of the country's ageing power system to handle such modern plants, an expert at a U.S. think tank said on Friday.
Ronald Hagen of the East-West Center told Reuters by telephone that North Korea was aware of the problem but at the same time might lack the funds to upgrade the power system.
North Korea agreed with the United States in 1994 to receive two Western-made light water nuclear reactors in exchange for freezing what the West suspected was its nuclear weapons programme.
The Korean Peninsular Energy Development Organization (KEDO), which groups the United States, South Korea and Japan, was formed a year later to finance the project.
Under the $5 billion agreement, two 1,000-megawatt capacity reactors would be delivered in 2003. KEDO and North Korea have yet to agree a site for the plants.

In a paper by Hagen on the North Korea energy sector this week, the East-West Center said: "It is difficult to assess the plans for the new reactor, though its development would necessitate considerable improvements of North Korea's existing power transmission system...The new reactors might be too big for the grid they are to serve."
The East-West Center is a Hawaii-based research group mostly funded by the U.S. government. It was set up in 1960 to help foster ties between the U.S. and the Asia-Pacific region.

North Korea's primary energy sector relies on coal and hydroelectric power. The East-West paper said North Korea has a generating capacity of around 11,000 megawatts of which about 7,000 is being used, although specific information was difficult to come by.
Nuclear power production would face serious difficulties, Hagen says in the paper.
Power is currently dispatched mechanically using telephones or telex because North Korea lacks computers.

"Nuclear power production requires a large, well-monitored and disciplined grid-which would not describe the current situation where dispatching is inefficient and system failures are frequent," Hagen wrote.

The report said "Until this system is improved, there is reason to question the suitability of the North Korean electrical system for sophisticated power plants. Specifically to be questioned would be nuclear power plants, which might suffer frequent trippings that could damage poorly maintained systems."
Hagen told Reuters that while KEDO was supplying the nuclear reactors, responsibility for a transmission infrastructure to support the nuclear reactors was outside its mandate.
And so long as North Korea remained insulated from the rest of the world, there was little prospect of the country being able to finance the upgrading of the existing system.
"It's a high risk if they do not find some way to encourage investment to come in. They are going to have to change something," he said.
